claim: Hippocampal place cells elevate their firing rates within circumscribed regions in the environment called 'place fields'.
source: Hippocampal place cells elevate their firing rates within circumscribed regions in the environment ('place fields') (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971

claim: Place cells display phase coding relative to the ~8 Hz theta oscillations of the hippocampal local field potential.
source: In addition to this firing rate code, place cells display phase coding relative to the ∼8 Hz theta oscillations of the hippocampal local field potential (LFP) (Vanderwolf, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanderwolf, 1969

claim: As animals cross a cell's place field, the cell fires at progressively earlier phases of the oscillation, a phenomenon known as theta phase precession.
source: As animals cross a cell's place field, the cell fires at progressively earlier phases of the oscillation, a phenomenon known as theta phase precession (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993

claim: Phase precession yields distinct neuronal sequences that traverse multiple positions within each cycle of the theta oscillation.
source: At the population level, phase precession yields distinct neuronal sequences that traverse multiple positions within each cycle of the theta oscillation.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the description of phase precession

claim: The first cells to fire in a theta cycle typically have place fields centered behind the current position of the animal, followed by cells with place fields centered progressively ahead, generating 'theta sequences'.
source: The first cells to fire typically have place fields centered behind the current position of the animal, followed by cells with place fields centered progressively ahead, generating so-called 'theta sequences' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2007 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The hippocampal theta code encompasses representations of past, present, and future events beyond just the current spatial location.
source: This phenomenon suggests that beyond the representation of the current spatial location of an animal, the hippocampal theta code more generally encompasses representations of past, present, and future events (Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Cei et al., 2014; Terada et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Cei et al., 2014; Terada et al., 2017

claim: Theta phase precession and theta sequences have been reported to respond to elapsed time.
source: In support of this, theta phase precession and theta sequences have been reported to respond to elapsed time (Pastalkova et al., 2008; Shimbo et al., 2021), particular events and behaviors including jumping (Lenck-Santini et al., 2008), pulling a lever, and sampling an object (Terada et al., 2017; Aronov et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pastalkova et al., 2008; Shimbo et al., 2021

claim: Phase-precession and theta sequences have been observed in brain regions other than the hippocampus.
source: Phase-precession and theta sequences have also been observed in brain regions other than the hippocampus (Kim et al., 2012; Hafting et al., 2008; Jones and Wilson, 2005; van der Meer and Redish, 2011; Tingley et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2012; Hafting et al., 2008; Jones and Wilson, 2005; van der Meer and Redish, 2011; Tingley et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2021

claim: The theta phase code plays a supporting role in sequential learning, prediction, and planning.
source: These studies indicate that the theta phase code plays a supporting role in a wide array of cognitive functions, such as sequential learning (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Skaggs et al., 1996; Reifenstein et al., 2021), prediction (Lisman and Redish, 2009; Kay et al., 2020), and planning (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bolding et al., 2020; Bush et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations for each cognitive function

claim: The relationship between theta phase, represented position, and the animal's true location has not previously been made explicit.
source: Surprisingly, this relationship has not previously been made explicit.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the literature

claim: The length of theta sweeps has been shown to increase proportionally with running speed.
source: One the one hand, the length of theta sweeps has been shown to increase proportionally with running speed (Maurer et al., 2012; Gupta et al., 2012), a result which is consistent with temporal sweeps.
evidence: Supported by citations to Maurer et al., 2012; Gupta et al., 2012

claim: Place field parameters such as place field size and phase precession slope do not change with speed.
source: On the other hand, place field parameters, such as place field size or the slope of the spikes' phase vs. position relationship (phase precession slope), do not change with speed (Huxter et al., 2003; Maurer et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2009; Geisler et al., 2007), which is consistent with spatial sweeps.
evidence: Supported by citations to Huxter et al., 2003; Maurer et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2009; Geisler et al., 2007

claim: Place fields are larger and have shallower phase precession slopes at locations where animals typically run faster.
source: Notably, we find that place fields are larger and have shallower phase precession slopes at locations where animals typically run faster, in support of the behavior-dependent sweep model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The behavior-dependent sweep model uniquely accounts for the combination of experimental findings at the population and single-cell levels.
source: Finally, we compare simulated data generated from the three models based on experimentally measured trajectories and theta oscillations, and confirm that the behavior-dependent sweep uniquely accounts for the combination of experimental findings at the population and single-cell levels.
evidence: Supported by model simulations and comparisons to experimental data

claim: In the spatial sweep model, both phase precession slopes and place field sizes are independent of running speed.
source: Both phase precession slopes and place field sizes are independent of running speed (Figure 1B), consistent with experimental observations (Huxter et al., 2003; Schmidt et al., 2009; Geisler et al., 2007; Sup. Fig. 1 in Maurer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by model predictions shown in Figure 1B and citations to experimental studies

claim: Experimental results show that theta trajectory length is roughly proportional to running speed for speeds above 5 cm/s.
source: Contrary to this prediction, experimental results show that the theta trajectory length is roughly proportional to running speed (Figure 2 in Maurer et al., 2012; Figure 1C in Gupta et al., 2012 for speeds above 5 cm/s).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maurer et al., 2012 and Gupta et al., 2012

claim: In the temporal sweep model, different phases of theta represent the positions that the animals have reached or will reach at some time interval in the past and future, respectively.
source: An alternative to the above is the temporal sweep model, where different phases of theta represent the positions that the animals have reached or will reach at some time interval in the past and future, respectively (see Itskov et al., 2008 for a similar model).
evidence: Theoretical description with citation to similar model by Itskov et al., 2008

claim: In the temporal sweep model, place field sizes increase and phase precession slopes become shallower with running speed.
source: However, at the single-cell level, the temporal sweep model predicts that place field sizes increase and phase precession slopes become shallower with running speed (Figure 1D) – in clear conflict with the experimental results mentioned above.
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 1D

claim: In the behavior-dependent sweep model, at different phases of theta, the place cell population represents the positions that would have been or would be reached at certain time intervals in the past or future, assuming the animal runs at the characteristic speed through each location.
source: According to this model, at different phases of theta, the place cell population represents the positions that would have been or would be reached at certain time intervals in the past or future, like in the temporal sweep, but under the assumption that the animal runs at the characteristic speed through each location, rather than at the instantaneous running speed (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Theoretical description illustrated in Figure 2A,B

claim: The study re-analyzed publicly available single unit recordings from CA1 of 6 rats running on linear tracks for water rewards at both ends.
source: To this end, we re-analyzed publicly available simultaneous single unit recordings from CA1 of 6 rats running on linear tracks for water rewards at both ends.
evidence: Description of experimental data used in the study

claim: Three of the experimental sessions were from tracks that were familiar to the animal while the remaining three were from novel tracks.
source: Three of the sessions (Mizuseki et al., 2013) were from tracks that were familiar to the animal while the remaining three Grosmark et al., 2016 were from novel tracks.
evidence: Description of experimental data sources

claim: The first 5 minutes of recordings on the novel track were discarded to ensure stable spatial representations and theta phase precession.
source: To ensure that spatial representations and theta phase precession were stable for the entirety of the periods under examination, we discarded the first 5 min of the recording on the novel track, allowing sufficient time for hippocampal place fields and phase precession to have stabilized (Frank et al., 2004; Cheng and Frank, 2008).
evidence: Methodological decision supported by citations to Frank et al., 2004; Cheng and Frank, 2008

claim: Theta trajectory lengths increased roughly proportionately to running speed in the experimental data.
source: Despite the high level of variability, it was clear in the individual rats' averages and in the grand average across animals that the trajectory lengths increased roughly proportionately to running speed (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental data analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Individual place fields tended to maintain similar sizes regardless of running speed.
source: Visual inspection revealed that individual fields tended to maintain similar sizes regardless of running speed (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental data analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: When combining data across fields, the average field size generally increases as a function of running speed.
source: Remarkably, when combining data across fields, the average field size generally increases as a function of running speed. Colored lines represent individual animals, and the thick black line averages over them.
evidence: Experimental data analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: The increase in place field sizes combined across fields is statistically significant for five of the six animals (p<0.02).
source: This increase in place field sizes is consistent with the temporal sweep model, whereas the lack of within-field changes mentioned above supports spatial sweeps. Both findings, however, can be consistent with the behavior-dependent sweep model provided that place fields are larger in track areas characterized by faster running (Figure 2). We examine this question below.
evidence: Statistical test results from experimental data analysis

claim: There was no significant relationship between phase precession slope and speed for individual fields in single-pass analysis.
source: There was no significant relationship between phase precession slope and speed for individual fields in any of the three animals with sufficient data for this analysis, that is, more than 10 fields (Figure 5E).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: All animals showed similar asymmetric inverted U-shape relationships between characteristic speed and position along the track.
source: All animals showed similar asymmetric inverted U-shape relationships between characteristic speed and position along the track.
evidence: Experimental data analysis

claim: Running speeds at each position were clustered around the characteristic running speed.
source: Next, as required by the second prerequisite, we confirmed that running speeds at each position were clustered around the characteristic running speed (Figure 6C).
evidence: Experimental data analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Inverted U-shape relationships were observed between position along the track and theta trajectory lengths and place field sizes.
source: We also observed inverted U-shape relationships between position along the track, and theta trajectory lengths and place field sizes (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Experimental data analysis shown in Figure 6D,E

claim: Theta trajectory lengths and place field sizes increased, and inverse phase precession slopes decreased, roughly in proportion to characteristic speed for up to at least 60 cm/s.
source: Finally, in support of the third prerequisite, we found that theta trajectory lengths and place field sizes increased, and inverse phase precession slopes decreased, roughly in proportion to characteristic speed for up to at least 60 cm/s, which encompassed most of the data (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: Experimental data analysis shown in Figure 6G–I

claim: Theta trajectory lengths, place field sizes and inverse phase precession slopes all displayed strikingly linear relationships to one another.
source: We found that the three of them displayed strikingly linear relationships to one another (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), underscoring the intimate relationships that hold between these systematically interrelated measures of place cell activity.
evidence: Experimental data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3

claim: Theta trajectory length correlates slightly better with characteristic running speed than with either mean place field size or mean inverse phase precession slope at the locations where the trajectories occurred (R = 0.35 vs 0.29).
source: It is also worth noting that theta trajectory length correlates slightly better with characteristic running speed than with either mean place field size or mean inverse phase precession slope at the locations where the trajectories occurred (R = 0.35 vs 0.29 for the latter two; Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,C

claim: Characteristic running speed uniquely accounted for 13% and 11% of the variance in place field sizes and inverse phase precession slopes, respectively, while distance to the border uniquely accounted for 3% and 7%.
source: A model combining both variables could account for 29% and 28% of the variance in place field sizes and inverse phase precession slopes, respectively. Out of this, characteristic running speed uniquely accounted for 13% and 11% of the variance, whereas distance to the border uniquely accounted for 3% and 7%, respectively.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The temporal sweep model provides a qualitative fit to the average theta trajectory lengths, place field sizes and phase precession slopes, but incorrectly predicts increases in individual place field sizes and phase precession slopes.
source: The temporal sweep model provides a qualitative fit to the average theta trajectory lengths, place field sizes and phase precession slopes, but incorrectly predicts increases in individual place field sizes and phase precession slopes.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 7B

claim: The spatial sweep model accounts for the lack of within-field increases in place field sizes and phase precession slopes, but the increase in theta trajectory length with running speed is not nearly large enough and place field sizes and phase precession slopes remain flat with running speed.
source: The spatial sweep model accounts for the lack of within-field increases in place field sizes and phase precession slopes. However, the increase in theta trajectory length with running speed is not nearly large enough and place field sizes and phase precession slopes remain flat with running speed.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 7C

claim: The behavior-dependent sweep model captures both the population average and within-field effects, providing a good agreement with all experimental results.
source: The behavior-dependent sweep model captures both the population average and within-field effects, providing a good agreement with all experimental results.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 7D

claim: The behavior-dependent sweep model produced values with the lowest mean squared deviation to the experimental data for four of the five variables considered.
source: Furthermore, the behavior-dependent sweep produced values with the lowest mean squared deviation to the experimental data for four of the five variables considered (Figure 7; numbers in corners).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of model predictions to experimental data shown in Figure 7

claim: The behavior-dependent sweep model replicates the experimentally observed increase in firing rates with running speed.
source: The behavior-dependent sweep model replicates the experimentally observed increase in firing rates with running speed.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: Reaction times for rats performing simple and choice tasks range between 150 ms and 500 ms.
source: Reaction times for rats performing simple and choice tasks range between 150 ms and 500 ms (Baunez et al., 2001; Brown and Robbins, 1991), and stop signal reaction times stand at around 360 ms (Eagle et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baunez et al., 2001; Brown and Robbins, 1991; Eagle et al., 2009

claim: Place fields increase in size along the dorsoventral axis of the hippocampus.
source: However, place fields (Kjelstrup et al., 2008) increase in size along the dorsoventral axis of the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kjelstrup et al., 2008

claim: The largest place fields recorded in rats stand at about 10 m, which would correspond to representing a time window of > 10 s.
source: The largest place fields recorded in rats stand at about 10 m, which would correspond to representing a time window of > 10 s.
evidence: Inference based on established knowledge about place field sizes

claim: Theta sequences are reportedly lacking or reduced during the first traversals through a novel environment.
source: Another possibility is that the characteristic speed is taken to be the speed of the firsts traversals through the environment, in which theta sequences are reportedly lacking or reduced (Feng et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2021), and then updated incrementally.
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2021

claim: Theta frequency has been shown to increase with positive acceleration, but not deceleration or speed.
source: Third, theta frequency has recently been shown to increase with positive acceleration, but not deceleration or speed (Kropff et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kropff et al., 2021

claim: The increase in theta frequency is accompanied by an increase in the intrinsic firing frequency of cells which would provide a compensatory effect on theta trajectories.
source: Furthermore, as shown by Kropff et al., 2021, the increase in theta frequency is accompanied by an increase in the intrinsic firing frequency of cells which would provide a compensatory effect on theta trajectories.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kropff et al., 2021

claim: Theta phase coding has been demonstrated in two-dimensional environments and in grid cells.
source: Lastly, our behavior-dependent sweep model could be applied to describing the activity of place cells in two-dimensional environments, and potentially also that of grid cells, since theta phase coding has been demonstrated in both of these cases (Huxter et al., 2008; Jeewajee et al., 2014; Hafting et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huxter et al., 2008; Jeewajee et al., 2014; Hafting et al., 2008

claim: The behavior-dependent sweep model predicts that sizes of individual firing fields within the grid will vary according to running speeds characteristic of the corresponding maze regions, while the distance between firing field peaks would remain constant.
source: For grid cells, our model predicts that sizes of individual firing fields within the grid will vary according to running speeds characteristic of the corresponding maze regions. By contrast, the distance between firing field peaks would remain constant, since the locations of the underlying true fields remain fixed in the model.
evidence: Prediction derived from the behavior-dependent sweep model
